food-approaching children are more likely to be overweight, while food-avoiding children are less likely to be overweight.
children’s appetitive characteristics are associated with weight and with dietary behaviours in the context of general parenting.
food-approaching and food-avoiding appetitive traits were related to child weight and dietary intake, and that authoritative parenting moderated these relations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the association between children’s appetitive behaviour and weight and dietary behaviour.
individual differences in child weight, and with the role of parenting in explaining these differences.
the role of appetitive traits in the development of obesity in childhood and adolescence.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
food-approaching traits are positively related to weight and fruit consumption, while food-avoiding traits are negatively related to weight and positively related to fruit consumption.
the associations between appetitiveness and child weight/intake depend on parenting style, which could be used to guide the design and development of preventive interventions.
children with food-approaching traits and/or authoritative parenting are at higher risk for overweight.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the more food approachable a child is, the more likely it is that he or she will have a higher BMI and eat less fruits.
we have shown that food-approaching children are more likely to be overweight and eat less fruit than food-avoidant children.
we have shown that children with appetitive traits are at increased risk for overweight.
The main takeaway from our work is that
children’s appetitive trait can be an important factor in determining children’s weight and intake.
children who show food-approaching behaviours (e.g. food responsiveness) are at increased risk for overweight, and children who show food avoiding behaviours are at reduced risk for overweight.
the way parents interact with children can affect the effect of appetive traits on child weight and dietary intake.
